Built in Alameda. Proven on the water.
Navier is not a concept. The platform proposed for the Bay is signed, funded and operating today — built by an MIT, NASA and GoogleX team in Alameda.
A 100-vessel national ferry network for the Maldives — on this same platform.
Deployed with the U.S. Navy and inside Leidos programs — proven beyond the demo dock.

Start small. Prove it on the water. WETA decides.
Source: WETA 2050 Service Vision and Expansion Policy
Three ways a small electric hydrofoil helps WETA’s existing plan — without changing who decides.
Add targeted frequency or a smaller capacity increment where WETA identifies a real rider need.
Give an emerging market a practical electric starting point while WETA learns demand and operations.
Put smaller stops closer to where trips start and end — reducing first/last-mile friction and making water transit useful to more riders.
Nine terminals — and a published plan for more
SF Bay Ferry runs a nine-terminal public network across the Bay and is moving its fleet toward zero-emission service.
Mission Bay · Treasure Island · Berkeley · Redwood City — expansion WETA has already put on the map.
Larkspur, Sausalito and Tiburon are served by Golden Gate Ferry — the Bay’s water network is already bigger than any one agency.

Marin terminals are operated by Golden Gate Ferry. Every link shown is illustrative and pending route, facility and demand studies with the agencies involved.
Three steps. WETA decides at every gate.
Demo flights from our Alameda home port, tested against WETA’s operating questions: safety case, energy and charging, reliability, ride quality, wake and noise, terminal interface.
Output: a shared operating report — not a procurement commitment.
WETA selects one bounded use case. We measure what matters: energy and cost per trip, availability, on-time performance, accessibility and rider experience.
Success and stop thresholds are agreed before launch.
Add frequency, vessels or a second route only on proven performance.
Every step follows WETA approval, procurement, terminal, labor and community processes.
Start small with the 8-passenger N30 — step up to the 20-passenger N45 and larger as demand proves out. The right-sized vessel for every route.
Sources: WETA pilot framework · Navier platform materials

Six questions we answer together — before the first rider boards
Is the USCG pathway and operating envelope clear?
Can boarding, seating, bikes, luggage and fare integration work?
Are berth access, shore power and turnaround practical?
Do weather, sea state, range reserve, wake and navigation meet requirements?
Can WETA train, staff, maintain and dispatch the service reliably?
Does lifecycle cost improve useful access and rider outcomes?
